question.text: The tax head of Silverline Capital is reviewing a proposed structure where an offshore Mauritius investor routes capital into an Indian Cat II AIF to invest in an Indian portfolio company. The arrangement's dominant purpose is to avoid Indian capital gains tax on the portfolio exit using the Mauritius treaty. Which ITA provision enables the tax authorities to disregard/recharacterise this structure?

answer.text: General Anti-Avoidance Rules (GAAR), effective 1 April 2017 — applies if main purpose is tax benefit AND one of four tainted elements is met (non-arm's-length, misuse of ITA, lacks commercial substance, bona fide-unusual manner)

explanation.text: The Logic: GAAR (Chapter X-A of the ITA, effective 1 April 2017) can be invoked if an arrangement's main purpose is a tax benefit AND satisfies any ONE of four tainted elements: (a) not-at-arm's-length rights/obligations, (b) misuse/abuse of ITA, (c) lacks commercial substance, (d) not employed for bona fide purposes in a manner not normally done. Treaty shopping via Mauritius for pure tax benefit squarely qualifies. Authorities can recharacterise, disregard, or reallocate. The LOB clause in a treaty can pre-empt GAAR in specific cases. The Trap: Option B — 115UB is pass-through mechanics, no recharacterisation power. Option C — 56(2)(x) deals with property at below-FMV. Option D is TDS, not recharacterisation. Cross-Exam Context: XV (Research Analyst) and XIX-A touch on GAAR lightly; XIX-C requires the manager to run a GAAR-risk checklist on fund structure and investor tax residence. Manager's Pro-Tip: Before activating a treaty benefit in your PPM, commission a GAAR opinion: (i) proof of commercial substance (employees, decisions on-ground), (ii) business rationale other than tax, (iii) LOB clause satisfaction. The Mauritius 2016 protocol already grandfathers pre-April-2017 investments; plan exits accordingly.
